**Key History**
Patient presented alone to the clinic with a 2-hour history of central crushing chest pain radiating to the left side, associated with significant diaphoresis, nausea, and jaw tightness. Patient drove themselves to the clinic. Emergency services have been advised and patient has agreed to call for an ambulance.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) — classic presentation: crushing central chest pain radiating left, jaw tightness, diaphoresis, nausea, 2-hour duration
2. Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) / Unstable Angina — same presentation, distinction requires ECG and troponins
3. Aortic dissection — crushing central chest pain can mimic ACS; radiation pattern and jaw involvement less typical but cannot be excluded

*Also consider:*
• Pulmonary embolism — can present with chest pain and diaphoresis, though crushing quality and jaw pain are less typical
• Severe GORD / oesophageal spasm — can mimic cardiac pain, but diaphoresis, nausea, and jaw tightness make this unlikely here

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Aortic dissection — if BP differential between arms is present or pain has any tearing/ripping component not yet elicited, this must be excluded urgently before thrombolysis
⚠ Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy — can present identically to ACS, particularly in post-menopausal women; ECG and echo needed

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Immediate 12-lead ECG — look for ST elevation, new LBBB, or ST depression
• Bilateral blood pressure measurement — asymmetry suggests aortic dissection
• Pulse oximetry and respiratory rate
• Auscultate heart and lungs — new murmur, S3, or pulmonary oedema
• Assess JVP and peripheral perfusion — signs of cardiogenic shock

*First line:*
• 12-lead ECG — immediate, look for STEMI pattern
• High-sensitivity troponin I or T — baseline now, repeat at 1 and 3 hours
• FBC, U&E, glucose, lipid profile
• Chest X-ray — widened mediastinum would raise concern for dissection

*If first line inconclusive:*
• CT pulmonary angiogram if PE suspected
• CT aortogram if dissection cannot be excluded clinically

**Management Principles**
• Call ahead to nearest cath lab / emergency cardiology — activate STEMI pathway if ECG confirms
• Aspirin 300mg stat (if no contraindication and dissection excluded)
• IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, oxygen if SpO2 < 94%
• Do NOT give thrombolytics until aortic dissection excluded
• Urgent transfer to emergency department — patient is alone and has been advised not to drive

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If ECG is non-diagnostic but symptoms persist, do not discharge — serial troponins and repeat ECG at 30–60 minutes are essential. A normal initial ECG does not exclude ACS.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Patient presents with a sudden-onset "thunderclap" headache, described as the worst headache of their life, onset approximately 3 hours ago. Patient is alone at home and has been advised to call emergency services. Full history was appropriately curtailed due to confirmed red flag — emergency escalation initiated.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) — classic thunderclap onset, "worst headache of life," sudden onset; this is SAH until proven otherwise.
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — can present with sudden severe headache; less common but important to exclude.
3. Hypertensive emergency with intracranial involvement — severe acute headache can accompany hypertensive crisis.

*Also consider:*
• Spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage — sudden severe headache, may have focal neurological signs.
• Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) — recurrent thunderclap headaches; can mimic SAH clinically.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Subarachnoid haemorrhage — sentinel bleed pattern; even if CT is initially negative, LP for xanthochromia is mandatory if clinical suspicion remains high. A normal CT does not exclude SAH.
⚠ Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — may be missed on standard CT; CT venography or MRI venography required if suspected.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full neurological examination including GCS, cranial nerves, motor and sensory assessment
• Fundoscopy — look for papilloedema or subhyaloid haemorrhage (strongly associated with SAH)
• Meningism assessment — neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
• Blood pressure both arms — hypertensive emergency must be identified and managed urgently
• Vital signs including temperature (to exclude infective meningitis)

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Urgent non-contrast CT head — to identify subarachnoid or intracerebral blood; best within 6 hours of onset
• If CT negative and clinical suspicion remains: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia and red cell count (ideally ≥ 12 hours post-onset for xanthochromia to be reliable)
• FBC, U&E, coagulation screen, blood glucose

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• CT angiography or MR angiography — to identify aneurysm, AVM, or RCVS
• MRI brain with FLAIR — may detect blood not visible on CT
• CT venography if cerebral venous sinus thrombosis suspected

**Management Principles**
• Emergency department transfer — already initiated
• Neurosurgical/neurology involvement urgently if SAH confirmed
• Strict bed rest, analgesia, anti-emetics as needed; avoid NSAIDs if SAH suspected
• Nimodipine if SAH confirmed — reduces vasospasm
• Do not administer anticoagulants until haemorrhagic cause excluded

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
A normal CT does not exclude SAH — if patient is seen at any point before full emergency workup, insist on LP for xanthochromia. If RCVS is diagnosed, counsel regarding triggers (exertion, sexual activity, Valsalva) and arrange neurology follow-up.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Young woman presenting with sudden-onset right iliac fossa pain that began periumbilically yesterday afternoon and migrated to the RIF — a classic migratory pattern. Pain is constant, dull, 6/10 and worsening, associated with nausea, low-grade fever (37.8°C), and anorexia. No vomiting, no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms, no PV bleeding or discharge. Notably, she is sexually active, not using contraception, and is 6 weeks amenorrhoeic — pregnancy must be excluded urgently.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Acute appendicitis** — classic migratory periumbilical to RIF pain, sudden onset, fever, anorexia, nausea, and progressive worsening over 24 hours is highly characteristic.
2. **Ectopic pregnancy** — 6 weeks amenorrhoea, no contraception, sexually active, RIF pain with nausea and low-grade fever; no PV bleeding does NOT exclude this — up to 50% of ectopic pregnancies present without bleeding initially.
3. **Ovarian pathology (torsion or ruptured ovarian cyst)** — sudden onset RIF pain in a young woman; torsion classically presents with sudden severe pain but can be more gradual; ruptured cyst may cause peritoneal irritation and low-grade fever.

*Also consider:*
• **Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)** — RIF pain, low-grade fever, nausea; absence of discharge doesn't exclude it; ask about cervical motion tenderness on examination.
• **Mesenteric adenitis** — can mimic appendicitis; more common in younger patients, often with recent viral illness.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Ectopic pregnancy** — this is the most dangerous diagnosis here and must be excluded before anything else. She is 6 weeks amenorrhoeic, unprotected sex, RIF pain. A ruptured ectopic can cause rapid haemodynamic collapse. Urine or serum βhCG is mandatory before any other workup.
⚠ **Appendicitis with impending perforation** — pain has been worsening for ~24 hours; if Rovsing's sign, rebound tenderness, or guarding is present, surgical referral is urgent.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Vital signs — temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation
• Abdominal examination: localise tenderness, check for guarding and rigidity, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, obturator sign
• Rebound tenderness — assess carefully; if present, raises concern for peritoneal irritation
• Pelvic examination — cervical motion tenderness (chandelier sign), adnexal tenderness or mass
• Bimanual pelvic exam to assess uterine size and adnexal masses

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Urine βhCG — urgent; must be done immediately to exclude pregnancy before proceeding
• FBC — look for leukocytosis (appendicitis, PID) or anaemia (ectopic bleeding)
• CRP — elevated in appendicitis and PID
• Urine dipstick and MC&S — to exclude UTI/pyelonephritis (no urinary symptoms but worth excluding)
• Pelvic USS — assess for intrauterine pregnancy, free fluid, adnexal mass, or appendix if visualised

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• Serum quantitative βhCG — if urine positive, helps assess viability and guide management
• CT abdomen/pelvis — if appendicitis is suspected and USS inconclusive (consider radiation in potentially pregnant patient — USS first)
• Repeat βhCG in 48 hours if initial result equivocal

**Management Principles**
• **If βhCG positive → treat as ectopic until proven otherwise** — urgent gynaecology referral, do not delay; nil by mouth pending surgical assessment
• If appendicitis confirmed or strongly suspected → urgent surgical referral; nil by mouth, IV

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Adult male (age not obtained — reception to confirm), presenting with a 3-week history of persistent fatigue, non-restorative sleep (5 hours/night, waking with racing thoughts), and generalised pressure-type headaches (4-5/10). Background of significant occupational stress, ~10 cigarettes/day for 20 years, and approximately 5 standard beers daily. Father had MI at 58. No known medical conditions, no regular medications. HIV never tested. No weight loss, fever, or focal neurological symptoms volunteered.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Alcohol use disorder / hazardous drinking** — 5 beers/day is well above safe limits and is itself sufficient to cause fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and daily headaches (morning headaches may represent mild withdrawal); this should be considered the primary driver until excluded
2. **Adjustment disorder / anxiety with somatic features** — significant occupational stress, racing thoughts at night, fatigue, and headaches are a classic presentation; sleep-onset insomnia with rumination is characteristic
3. **Major depressive disorder** — fatigue, poor sleep, low energy, reduced activity, and general anhedonia ("feeling blah") meet several DSM criteria; PHQ-9 scoring would be useful

*Also consider:*
• **Obstructive sleep apnoea** — non-restorative sleep, daytime fatigue, and alcohol use (which worsens OSA) make this plausible; ask about snoring and witnessed apnoeas
• **Hypothyroidism** — fatigue, low energy, and headaches in a middle-aged adult; TSH is a quick and cheap screen
• **Anaemia** — chronic fatigue, pallor, exertional symptoms; FBC essential
• **Hypertension** — strong family history (father MI at 58), alcohol use, smoking, and stress are all risk factors; headaches may be hypertensive; BP must be checked today

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Hypertensive urgency/early end-organ involvement** — given family history, lifestyle factors, and new-onset headaches, BP must be measured as a priority today; if significantly elevated with headaches, this changes management immediately
⚠ **Hazardous/harmful alcohol use as primary diagnosis** — 5 beers/day (~35 units/week, well above the 14-unit safe limit) may be underreported; consider AUDIT-C screening; withdrawal headaches and fatigue are frequently missed in this context
⚠ **Early HIV-related illness** — patient has never tested; fatigue and general malaise are common early presentations; strongly recommend offering a rapid HIV test today given the opportunity

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Blood pressure (both arms) — priority given headaches and family/lifestyle risk
• Pulse rate and rhythm
• BMI and waist circumference
• Thyroid palpation
• Conjunctival pallor (screen for anaemia)
• Abdominal examination — hepatomegaly given alcohol use
• Brief neurological screen — cranial nerves, coordination, if any focal symptoms emerge

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• FBC — screen for anaemia, infection
• TSH — exclude hypothyroidism
• Fasting glucose and HbA1c — given lifestyle and family history
• Lipogram — cardiovascular risk (father MI at 58, smoker, alcohol)
• LFTs and GGT — alcohol-related hepatic involvement
• Urea and electrolytes, creatinine — baseline
• Rapid HIV test — offer today; patient has never been tested
• Urinalysis

*If first line inconclusive:*
• Ferritin and iron studies — if FBC suggests iron deficiency
• Sleep study referral — if OSA suspected after clinical assessment
• PHQ-9 formal scoring — if depression remains a leading diagnosis

**Management Principles**
• Measure and address blood pressure today — if elevated, initiate antihypertensive and lifestyle counselling
• Alcohol brief intervention (AUDIT-C / FRAMES approach) — 5 beers/day is hazardous

**Key History**
Young adult male (lives with housemates, socially active, gym-goer) presenting with a 3-day history of acute-onset dull lower back pain, rated 5/10, aggravated by movement and bending, partially relieved by rest. No radiation to legs, groin, or abdomen. No bladder or bowel dysfunction. No neurological symptoms (no leg weakness or numbness). No prior back problems. Partially managed with paracetamol 500mg (taken twice since yesterday).

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. Acute mechanical lower back pain — sudden onset, activity-related, no neurological features, young active male, gym history; classic presentation
2. Lumbar muscle strain — consistent with gym activity, sudden onset, dull aching quality, movement-aggravated
3. Facet joint sprain — acute onset with bending/movement aggravation, no radiculopathy

*Also consider:*
• Disc prolapse (early/mild) — no radiculopathy currently, but worth checking for subtle signs on examination given acute onset
• Sacroiliac joint dysfunction — common in young active adults, can present as unilateral dull lower back pain

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Cauda equina syndrome — currently no bladder/bowel dysfunction or leg neurology, but this must be actively excluded on examination given acute onset; any saddle anaesthesia or urinary retention warrants urgent referral
⚠ Vertebral fracture — no trauma history elicited (consider asking in appointment if heavy lifting or contact sport is involved)
⚠ Renal pathology (e.g. renal calculus, pyelonephritis) — no lateral radiation or fever reported, but worth excluding given acute onset; check for costovertebral angle tenderness on examination

• Full neurological lower limb exam: power, sensation, reflexes (L3–S1), straight leg raise bilaterally
• Palpation of lumbar spine and paraspinal muscles for point tenderness
• Costovertebral angle percussion to exclude renal origin
• Assess range of motion (flexion, extension, lateral rotation)
• Check for saddle area sensation if any concern arises in consultation

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• None immediately required if examination confirms uncomplicated mechanical back pain — clinical diagnosis

*If first line inconclusive or red flags emerge:*
• Urinalysis — to exclude renal/urinary cause
• Lumbar X-ray — if fracture or bony pathology suspected
• MRI lumbar spine — if neurological signs emerge or no improvement after 4–6 weeks

**Management Principles**
• Reassure and encourage early return to gentle activity (avoid bed rest)
• Optimise analgesia: regular paracetamol 1g QID + consider short course of an NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen with food) if no contraindications
• Consider adding a short course of muscle relaxant (e.g. cyclobenzaprine) if muscle spasm prominent on examination
• Advise temporary modification of gym activity — avoid heavy lifting and spinal loading until resolved
• Safety net: return immediately if bladder/bowel symptoms develop, leg weakness/numbness, or pain significantly worsens

If patient returns with any bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, or escalating pain unresponsive to analgesia — consider cauda equina syndrome and refer to emergency immediately.

**Key History**
32-week pregnant G2P1 (previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery) presenting with acute onset of severe headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights), right upper quadrant/sub-costal pain, and facial and hand oedema — all commencing around 08:00 this morning. Additionally reports reduced fetal movements today. Patient has attended 5 antenatal visits. Patient has been redirected to emergency services with husband accompanying.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Pre-eclampsia with severe features** — classic tetrad of severe headache, visual disturbance, RUQ pain, and facial/hand oedema at 32 weeks gestation; reduced fetal movements adds urgency
2. **HELLP Syndrome** — RUQ/epigastric pain at this gestation with the above features raises strong suspicion for haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets; can occur with or without hypertension
3. **Eclampsia (impending)** — severe headache + visual symptoms in this context represent a pre-seizure picture until proven otherwise

*Also consider:*
• **Acute fatty liver of pregnancy** — RUQ pain, malaise at third trimester; rarer but can mimic HELLP
• **Biliary colic / acute cholecystitis** — RUQ pain in pregnancy is not always pre-eclampsia; however, the full constellation here makes obstetric cause far more likely

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **HELLP Syndrome** — RUQ pain is the key feature that elevates this beyond uncomplicated pre-eclampsia; can deteriorate rapidly to hepatic rupture, DIC, and maternal death
⚠ **Placental abruption** — reduced fetal movements in the context of severe pre-eclampsia raises concern for abruption; requires urgent CTG and obstetric assessment

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
*(For emergency team's reference)*
• Blood pressure — both arms; MAP calculation
• Fundoscopy — papilloedema, arteriovenous changes
• Abdominal palpation — uterine tenderness, fundal height, fetal lie and presentation
• Hepatic tenderness — right hypochondrium
• Deep tendon reflexes — hyperreflexia suggests impending eclampsia; clonus is ominous
• Urinalysis — proteinuria (dipstick as minimum)
• Fetal heart rate and CTG — urgent given reduced movements

**Investigations**
*First line (urgent):*
• BP measurement — likely severely elevated
• Urine dipstick for protein → MSU
• FBC — thrombocytopaenia in HELLP
• LFTs — elevated transaminases in HELLP/hepatic involvement
• LDH and uric acid — haemolysis markers
• Coagulation screen (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen) — DIC screen
• Urea and creatinine — renal involvement
• CTG — reduced fetal movements requires immediate electronic fetal monitoring
• Obstetric ultrasound — fetal wellbeing, amniotic fluid index, placental assessment

*If first line inconclusive:*
• MRI brain if neurological symptoms persist post-delivery (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome — PRES)
• Doppler studies — umbilical artery and middle cerebral artery if fetal compromise suspected

**Management Principles**
• This patient requires immediate tertiary obstetric emergency care — she has been directed to ER with her husband
• Antihypertensive therapy if BP ≥ 160/110 (IV labetalol, oral nifedipine, or IV hydralazine per local protocol)
• Magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis given severe features
• Corticosteroids (betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity at 32 weeks if delivery anticipated
• Urgent obstetric and neonatology team involvement — likely delivery within 24–48 hours depending on maternal and fetal status
• HDU/ICU level monitoring

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*

2. Acute purulent bronchitis — productive cough post-viral with fever; however, exertional breathlessness raises concern beyond simple bronchitis
3. Post-viral/secondary bacterial sinobronchial infection — purulent sputum post-cold, fever; possible if examination doesn't confirm consolidation

*Also consider:*
• Influenza with bacterial superinfection — timing fits (cold 2 weeks ago, worsening); fever and purulent sputum consistent
• Whooping cough (pertussis) — less likely given purulent sputum and fever, but worth considering if cough has a paroxysmal quality not captured in history

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Pulmonary TB — night sweats and weight loss denied, no known contacts, but SA context mandates consideration; sputum AFB if no improvement with standard antibiotics

• Check for signs of pleurisy (pleural rub)
• Assess hydration status

*First line:*
• Chest X-ray — to confirm or exclude consolidation, effusion, or other pathology
• Full blood count — elevated WCC with neutrophilia would support bacterial infection; lymphocytosis may suggest viral

• Sputum culture and sensitivity — especially if she fails to respond to first-line antibiotics

2. **Chlamydial or Gonococcal cervicitis** — yellow purulent discharge, odour, pelvic discomfort. Both are common STIs presenting this way; PID is frequently a complication of untreated cervicitis.
3. **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** — abnormal discharge with unpleasant (often fishy) odour is the hallmark. However, BV less typically causes lower abdominal pain — the pain here makes an upper genital tract infection more likely.

• Bimanual pelvic examination — cervical motion tenderness (chandelier sign), adnexal tenderness or masses, uterine tenderness
• Check for left adnexal mass suggestive of TOA or ovarian pathology

• Wet prep / microscopy — Trichomonas vaginalis

**Key History**
Young adult student presenting with a 3-day history of severe sore throat (8/10 pain), odynophagia, fever of 38.7°C, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy, without cough or coryza. Lives in student residence; roommate had a similar illness last week. No past medical history, no regular medications, HIV-naïve. Single dose of paracetamol 1g taken this morning.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis** — classic Centor criteria present: fever, tonsillar exudate (possible, not visualised), tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough. Score ≥3 warrants treatment or throat swab.
2. **Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV)** — student age, residence setting, severe odynophagia, marked lymphadenopathy, high fever, and absence of cough all fit. Must be actively excluded before prescribing amoxicillin/ampicillin.
3. **Viral pharyngitis (non-EBV)** — adenovirus, other respiratory viruses can cause severe pharyngitis with fever; however absence of coryza and cough makes this less likely.

*Also consider:*
• **Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)** — severity of pain, difficulty swallowing, and 3-day progression warrant careful examination for uvular deviation, unilateral tonsillar bulging, and muffled/hot potato voice.
• **Fusobacterium necrophorum pharyngitis** — increasingly recognised in young adults, can progress to Lemierre's syndrome; consider if no improvement with standard treatment.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Peritonsillar abscess** — if uvular deviation or unilateral swelling present on examination, urgent ENT referral required; do not discharge without ruling this out given severity of symptoms.
⚠ **Lemierre's syndrome** — rare but life-threatening in young adults with severe pharyngitis; if neck swelling, rigors, or signs of sepsis present, urgent investigation and referral warranted.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Inspect oropharynx carefully: tonsillar size, presence of exudate, uvular position, unilateral bulging suggesting peritonsillar abscess
• Palpate cervical lymph nodes: size, tenderness, distribution (anterior vs posterior chain — posterior chain more typical of EBV)
• Check for splenomegaly (important if EBV suspected — contact sports restriction)
• Check for palatal petechiae (classic EBV sign)
• Vital signs: temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation
• General appearance: degree of distress, ability to open mouth fully (trismus suggests quinsy)

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Rapid strep antigen test or throat swab for culture — to confirm/exclude GAS
• FBC with differential — lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes supports EBV; neutrophilia supports bacterial infection
• Monospot test (heterophile antibody) — if EBV suspected clinically

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM/IgG, EA, EBNA) if monospot negative but clinical suspicion remains high
• Neck ultrasound if peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess suspected

**Management Principles**
• If GAS confirmed or Centor score ≥3 and EBV excluded: prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) — **avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin until EBV excluded** (risk of morbilliform rash)
• Adequate analgesia: regular paracetamol 1g QID; consider adding ibuprofen if no contraindications
• Ensure adequate hydration — advise cold fluids, ice chips
• If peritonsillar abscess confirmed: urgent ENT referral for drainage
• Advise no contact sport until EBV excluded and splenom

**Key History**
Adult patient presenting with a 2-year history of relapsing and remitting pruritic rash localised to the arms and behind the knees. The rash is red, dry, and occasionally crusted, with significant itch as the predominant symptom. It worsens in winter and with psychological stress, and has responded partially to topical corticosteroids. Notable family history of atopy (daughter with asthma, sister with hay fever). *Most likely:*
1. **Atopic dermatitis (eczema)** — classic flexural distribution (antecubital/popliteal fossae), chronic relapsing course, intense itch, dry/crusted skin, winter and stress triggers, personal atopic predisposition, strong family history of atopy, response to topical corticosteroids.
2. **Contact dermatitis (allergic or irritant)** — recent switch to biological washing powder is a significant trigger; however, the 2-year history predates this, so the washing powder is more likely exacerbating an underlying condition rather than being the sole cause.
3. **Psoriasis** — can present with dry, red, thickened plaques; flexural psoriasis is a recognised subtype. Less likely given the marked itch and family atopic history, but worth excluding clinically.

*Also consider:*
• **Scabies** — intense itch, can affect flexural areas; however, the chronic 2-year relapsing course and family atopy history make this less likely. Worth considering if burrows are visible or close contacts affected.
• **Cat dander allergy exacerbating atopic dermatitis** — patient has had the cat for 3 years, which overlaps with the 2-year history; worth exploring whether symptoms began around or after acquiring the cat.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides)** — can mimic chronic eczema for years; if lesions are not responding adequately to treatment, are morphologically atypical, or persist despite adequate therapy, consider skin biopsy to exclude.

• Full skin examination — document distribution, morphology (erythema, lichenification, excoriation, crusting), and extent of involvement using SCORAD or IGA score.

• Check for signs of lichenification (skin thickening from chronic scratching).

• Vital signs including temperature if secondary infection suspected.

*First line:*
• Clinical diagnosis — atopic dermatitis is primarily clinical; no immediate investigation required if presentation is classic.

**Key History**
31-year-old male, non-smoker, no regular medications, no significant past medical history, presenting with a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure this morning. Witnessed by wife — tonic phase followed by clonic phase, lasting approximately 2 minutes. Patient has no recall of the event; post-ictal confusion and generalised headache noted on recovery, headache now mostly resolved. Precipitating factors: significant sleep deprivation the night prior (approximately 3 hours). No alcohol, no illicit substances mentioned, no family history of epilepsy, HIV negative.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. First unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure (possible new-onset epilepsy) — classic tonic-clonic semiology, post-ictal confusion, no clear provocation beyond sleep deprivation; age of onset consistent with adult-onset epilepsy
2. Provoked seizure secondary to sleep deprivation — significant sleep deprivation is a well-recognised seizure precipitant; if this is the sole cause, risk of recurrence is lower, but this remains a diagnosis of exclusion
3. Symptomatic seizure secondary to an underlying structural or metabolic cause — first seizure in a previously healthy young adult warrants exclusion of intracranial pathology, electrolyte disturbance, or metabolic derangement

*Also consider:*
• Hypoglycaemia-provoked seizure — not directly asked about food/fluid intake preceding the event; worth clarifying
• Recreational drug or substance use (including withdrawal) — patient denied alcohol the night before but recreational substances not explicitly asked about; worth a sensitive direct question in consultation

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Intracranial pathology (space-occupying lesion, AVM, cortical dysplasia) — first seizure in a young adult with no family history mandates neuroimaging; post-ictal headache, while non-specific, should not be dismissed
⚠ Hypertensive encephalopathy or accelerated hypertension — blood pressure not yet obtained; essential in a first seizure workup
⚠ CNS infection (encephalitis, meningitis) — post-ictal headache and confusion noted; meningism must be assessed clinically even in the absence of fever

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full neurological examination including cranial nerves, coordination, pronator drift, reflexes, plantar responses — looking for any focal deficit suggesting structural lesion
• Assess for meningism: neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
• Blood pressure both arms — hypertension as a contributing or causative factor
• Tongue/cheek lacerations, shoulder tenderness (posterior dislocation is a classic post-seizure injury), urinary incontinence history
• General examination: skin for neurocutaneous stigmata (café-au-lait spots, ash-leaf macules suggesting tuberous sclerosis or neurofibromatosis)

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Capillary blood glucose — exclude hypoglycaemia as precipitant
• FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, magnesium, phosphate — metabolic/electrolyte causes
• ECG — exclude prolonged QT or Brugada pattern mimicking seizure
• Urine dipstick

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• MRI brain with and without contrast (preferred over CT for first seizure in a young adult — better cortical and structural resolution); CT head if MRI not immediately available or if urgent structural cause needs exclusion
• EEG — ideally within 24–48 hours; sleep-deprived EEG increases yield
• Lumbar puncture if meningism present or encephalitis suspected

**Management Principles**

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Female patient presenting with a 1-day history of right eye redness, itching, and a gritty sensation, with yellow crusty discharge particularly in the mornings. Vision is unaffected, no photophobia, and no deep eye pain. Her son had an identical presentation one week ago, suggesting a contagious aetiology. No past ocular history, no regular medications. Penicillin allergy (rash).

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Bacterial conjunctivitis** — unilateral onset, mucopurulent yellow discharge, crusting on waking, gritty/itchy sensation, clear household contact. Classic presentation.
2. **Viral conjunctivitis** — can also present with redness and discharge (though typically more watery); household spread is common with adenovirus. Discharge here is more purulent, which leans away from viral, but cannot be excluded.
3. **Allergic conjunctivitis** — prominent itching fits; however, no known allergen exposure, no bilateral involvement, no associated rhinitis, and household contact makes this less likely.

*Also consider:*
• **Chlamydial/gonococcal conjunctivitis** — typically more severe purulent discharge and may be associated with sexual history; worth considering if bacterial conjunctivitis fails to respond to standard treatment.
• **Blepharitis** — can cause crusting and grittiness, though usually bilateral and chronic; less likely given acute onset and household contact.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Acute angle-closure glaucoma** — no deep pain, no halos, no nausea, no visual change; effectively excluded by history, but worth a brief IOP check if any doubt on examination.
⚠ **Herpes simplex keratitis** — can mimic conjunctivitis; absence of photophobia and clear vision are reassuring, but examine the cornea carefully for dendritic ulceration, especially before prescribing topical steroids.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Visual acuity both eyes (Snellen chart)
• Examine conjunctiva and sclera for injection pattern — diffuse vs. circumcorneal (ciliary flush suggests deeper pathology)
• Examine cornea with fluorescein and blue light for dendritic ulcers or abrasions
• Evert upper eyelid to check for follicles (viral) vs. papillae (bacterial/allergic)
• Check for preauricular lymphadenopathy (common in viral/chlamydial conjunctivitis)
• Check IOP if any clinical uncertainty
• Vital signs: temperature

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Conjunctival swab for MC&S if discharge is heavy, atypical, or fails to respond to initial treatment — not routinely required for classic bacterial conjunctivitis in primary care.

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• Chlamydia/gonorrhoea PCR swab if presentation is unusually severe or recurrent, or if STI risk factors identified in consultation.

**Management Principles**
• Topical antibiotic eye drops — chloramphenicol is first line in SA primary care (not penicillin-based; safe given her allergy). Fusidic acid gel is an alternative.
• Advise strict hand hygiene and avoid sharing towels/pillowcases to limit household spread — son may need assessment too.
• Advise against contact lens wear until fully resolved.
• Safety net: return if vision changes, deep pain develops, photophobia appears, or no improvement within 5–7 days.
• No systemic treatment required unless gonococcal conjunctivitis suspected.

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If patient returns with reduced visual acuity, photophobia, or ciliary flush on re-examination, consider herpetic keratitis or anterior uveitis and refer urgently to ophthalmology. If no response to topical antibiotics within 5–7 days, consider chlamydial aetiology and treat accordingly (systemic azithromycin or doxycycline).

Since this morning, really. He was playing outside and that's when it started.

Not that we know of, no.
Got it. Has Liam ever been diagnosed with asthma, or has anything like this ever happened before?
No, this is the first time. He's never had asthma or anything like this before.
Right, got it. Does he have any other symptoms along with the wheeze — like a cough, fever, or a runny nose?
He's got a bit of a cough, yeah. No fever though. He actually had a cold last week, so maybe that's connected.

I see, that's useful to know.

Is the cough dry and tickly, or is he bringing up any phlegm?
It's more of a dry cough, I'd say. Not bringing anything up.
Okay, thanks. Has he been around any animals, dust, or anything else outside that might have triggered it — or is this just a normal garden?
We've got a dog at home, and it was really windy today when he was out playing. Could be either of those, I suppose.

Right, got it — those are both worth mentioning to the doctor.

Is Liam on any medicines at the moment — anything at all, even just for the cold last week?
No, we haven't given him anything. No medicines at all.
Okay, thanks. Are his vaccinations up to date?
Yes, they're all up to date.

Good to know.

Is Liam's breathing settled enough that he's comfortable right now, or does he seem to be working hard to breathe?
No, he's not working hard at it. He's still comfortable, just got this tight chest and you can hear the wheeze when he breathes out. He's not too distressed.

That's good to hear — thank you.

Has anyone in the family — either side — got asthma, allergies, or eczema?
Yeah, actually — I've got asthma myself.

I see, that's really helpful to know.

Does Liam have any skin conditions like eczema, or does he get hayfever at all?
Not that we've noticed, no. He doesn't have eczema or hayfever as far as we know.

Okay, thanks. Before I pass everything over to the doctor, I just have three quick general questions.

How has Liam been sleeping lately — does he seem rested when he wakes up?
He's been sleeping fine, yeah. No problems there.
Good. And how has he been in himself emotionally — has he seemed his usual happy self, or has he been stressed or upset about anything lately?
He's been his normal self, really. Happy and playing as usual — until this wheeze started this morning.
That's good to hear. And does Liam get plenty of physical activity during the week — running around, playing outside, that sort of thing?
Yeah, he's quite active. He's always outside playing, running around. That's actually what he was doing when this started today.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
5-year-old male presenting with first episode of expiratory wheeze and dry cough, onset this morning during outdoor play on a windy day. No fever, no respiratory distress, speaking in full sentences, comfortable at rest. Recent URTI last week. Known dog at home. Strong first-degree family history of asthma (mother). No prior diagnosis of asthma, eczema, or allergic rhinitis. No medications. Vaccinations up to date.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **First presentation of asthma** — classic age of onset, expiratory wheeze, post-viral trigger (recent URTI), exercise/wind trigger, first-degree relative with asthma, atopic triad not yet fully expressed but family history strongly supportive.
2. **Viral-induced wheeze (post-infectious bronchospasm)** — recent URTI directly preceding wheeze; common in pre-school age children; may or may not progress to true asthma.
3. **Allergic bronchospasm** — dog at home, windy outdoor environment; possible aeroallergen exposure as trigger; consistent with atopic predisposition given maternal asthma.

*Also consider:*
• **Foreign body aspiration** — sudden onset wheeze during outdoor play in a 5-year-old; however, expiratory wheeze is bilateral and he is comfortable, making this less likely but worth excluding clinically.
• **Reactive airways disease post-viral URTI** — transient bronchial hyperreactivity following viral illness, which may resolve without ongoing asthma diagnosis.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Foreign body aspiration** — onset during active outdoor play, sudden wheeze; even though he is comfortable, auscultate carefully for unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry; if any suspicion, chest X-ray with expiratory film or referral is warranted.
⚠ **First presentation of asthma in a child who may deteriorate** — currently stable but this is undiagnosed and unmedicated; no reliever inhaler at home. Advise parent on warning signs and when to go to emergency.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full respiratory exam — auscultate for bilateral vs. unilateral wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, air entry symmetry
• Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), heart rate
• Check for use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, subcostal/intercostal recession
• Examine skin for eczema (may be subtle — check behind knees, elbows, neck)
• Check nasal mucosa for allergic rhinitis signs
• Throat and ears — residual signs of recent URTI

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Clinical diagnosis at this stage — spirometry not reliable in a 5-year-old
• Consider peak flow if cooperative (though norms for age are limited)
• Chest X-ray — if any suspicion of foreign body, asymmetric wheeze, or poor response to bronchodilator; also useful baseline for first presentation

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• Skin prick testing or specific IgE (RAST) for dog dander, house dust mite, grass/pollen — can be arranged at follow-up to confirm atopic background
• Referral to paediatric pulmonology if wheeze recurs or diagnosis remains uncertain

**Management Principles**
• Trial of inhaled short-acting beta-agonist (salbutamol) — assess response in-room; this will also help confirm bronchospasm as the aetiology
• If response confirmed: prescribe salbutamol MDI with spacer and age-appropriate mask; educate parent on correct technique
• Discuss asthma action plan and when to seek emergency care (increased work of breathing, unable to speak in sentences, not responding to reliever)
• If this is a first asthma presentation: consider whether to start inhaled corticosteroid (preventer) — may defer to follow-up depending on response and frequency
• Advise on potential triggers: dog dander, wind/pollen, viral illness; consider referral for allergy testing
• Follow-up in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
17-year-old male presenting with 3 days of left-sided sharp, stabbing chest pain, onset approximately one day after an unusually intense bout of push-ups. Pain is localised, non-radiating, reproducible on palpation, and worsened by deep inspiration and movement. No associated sweating, nausea, palpitations, cough, fever, or shortness of breath. No medications, no allergies, no significant family or personal medical history.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Musculoskeletal chest pain / costochondritis** — sharp, localised, reproducible on palpation, worsened by movement and deep breathing, directly following overexertion with push-ups. Classic presentation.
2. **Intercostal muscle strain** — same mechanism, overlapping presentation; strain of intercostal or pectoral muscles from excessive push-ups is very consistent with this history.
3. **Costochondral injury** — repetitive strain from push-ups could cause costochondral junction irritation, presenting identically.

*Also consider:*
• **Precordial catch syndrome (Texidor's twitch)** — common in adolescents, sharp left-sided chest pain worsened by deep breathing, typically brief but can recur; benign.
• **Stress-related somatic symptoms** — significant matric exam stress noted; anxiety can amplify or contribute to chest pain perception, though the mechanical trigger makes this less likely as the primary cause.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Spontaneous pneumothorax** — young, tall/thin males are at risk; sharp left-sided pain worsened by breathing could fit. No breathlessness reported, but a small pneumothorax can present with minimal dyspnoea. Auscultate carefully and consider CXR if any doubt.
⚠ **Myocarditis / pericarditis** — though no viral prodrome reported, these can present in adolescents with sharp pleuritic chest pain. ECG and inflammatory markers warranted if examination is not clearly musculoskeletal.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Palpate the chest wall systematically — specifically the costochondral junctions, intercostal spaces, and left pectoral area to reproduce the pain and confirm musculoskeletal origin.
• Auscultate both lung fields carefully for reduced air entry or pleural rub.
• Auscultate the heart for a pericardial friction rub.
• Vitals: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, temperature.
• Observe chest wall symmetry and respiratory excursion.

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• **ECG** — to exclude pericarditis (saddle-shaped ST elevation, PR depression) or any arrhythmia.
• **Chest X-ray** — to exclude pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• **FBC and CRP/ESR** — to screen for inflammatory process suggesting myocarditis or pericarditis.
• **Troponin** — if any clinical concern for myocarditis remains after ECG and examination.

**Management Principles**
• If musculoskeletal confirmed: reassure, short course of NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen with food), rest from strenuous upper body exercise for 1–2 weeks, gradual return to activity.
• Counsel on appropriate progression of exercise intensity — relevant given exam stress and motivation to train harder.
• Brief check-in on exam stress and sleep — already identified; consider brief supportive counselling or referral if stress worsens.
• HIV counselling and testing can be offered routinely at this visit.

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If patient returns with worsening breathlessness, fever, or pain not improving with NSAIDs after 1 week, consider repeat CXR and inflammatory markers to exclude evolving pericarditis or missed pneumothorax.

conversation.content: I've been feeling very low since my baby was born 6 weeks ago.

I'm really glad you reached out — and it takes courage to talk about this. You're not alone in feeling this way after having a baby.

Can I ask — over the past two weeks, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?

*eyes welling up slightly*

Yeah... almost every day, really. I just feel so sad and hopeless, and I don't understand why because my baby is healthy and everything went fine with the birth.

I hear you — and please know that what you're feeling is real, regardless of how the birth went or how healthy your baby is. Take whatever time you need.

Over the past two weeks, have you had little interest or pleasure in doing things you'd normally enjoy?

*voice quiet and flat*

Yeah, I... I don't really enjoy anything anymore. Even with the baby — I feel like I should be happy, but I'm just... numb, I guess.

Thank you for telling me that — it means a lot that you're sharing this, and there's no right or wrong way to feel.

How has your sleep been — are you getting any rest at all, even when the baby sleeps?

*shakes head sadly*

Not really. Even when the baby's sleeping, I just lie there awake. My mind won't quiet down, and I feel so guilty about everything... I can't seem to switch off.

That sounds exhausting — not just physically, but emotionally too. The guilt especially can be so heavy to carry.

How have your energy levels been — do you have enough energy to get through the day?

*sighs heavily*

No, not really. I'm exhausted all the time, even though I'm not doing much. Everything just feels so hard — even basic things like getting out of bed or showering feel like too much.

I understand — when even small things take everything you've got, that's really tough.

How has your appetite been — are you managing to eat regularly?

*pauses, thinking*

I mean... I eat when I remember to, but I don't really feel hungry. My partner has to remind me sometimes. I just... I don't care much about it.

Okay, thank you for sharing that.

How has your ability to concentrate been — are you finding it hard to focus on things?

*nods slowly*

Yeah, it's hard to concentrate on anything. My thoughts just go all over the place, and I can't seem to focus on what I'm doing — even when I'm with the baby, I feel like my mind's somewhere else.

I hear you — that must make everything feel even harder.

How have you been feeling about yourself lately — do you find yourself being hard on yourself or feeling like you're not good enough?

*voice breaking slightly*

All the time. I feel like such a bad mother — like I'm failing at everything. I can't bond with her properly, and I just feel so guilty constantly, like I'm doing everything wrong.

Please hear me when I say — the fact that you care this much shows what a loving mother you are. Those feelings of guilt are part of what you're going through, not a reflection of the truth.

I need to ask you something important, and I want you to know it's a question we ask everyone who's feeling this low — sometimes when people feel this way, they have thoughts of hurting themselves or ending their life. Have you had any thoughts like that?

*shakes head firmly*

No, I haven't. I wouldn't... I could never do that. And I'd never hurt my baby either — I love her, even though I don't feel it right now. I'm just... I'm struggling, but I'm not thinking about that.

I'm really glad to hear that, and I believe you. And what you just said — that you love her even when you can't feel it right now — that's not nothing. That matters.

I do need to ask one more thing separately — have you had any thoughts of hurting your baby?

*looks up, eyes clear and serious*

No, absolutely not. Never. I would never hurt her — she's innocent and I love her. I just feel like I'm not a good enough mother for her, like she'd be better off without me around, but I would never... no.

Thank you for being so clear about that — and I hear you.

I do want to gently check on something you just said — when you say she'd be better off without you around, can you tell me a little more about what you mean by that?

*pauses, tears streaming down*

I just... I feel like I'm failing her. Like she deserves a better mum, one who can actually bond with her and enjoy her. I'm so numb and sad all the time, and I feel like that's affecting her somehow, like she's better off not having me dragging her down with all my sadness.

*voice quieter*

But I know that's not... I'm not thinking about leaving or anything like that. I just feel guilty, like I'm not good enough for her.

Thank you for explaining that — and I hear you clearly. That's a feeling of not being enough, not a thought of leaving. That makes sense, and it's something the doctor will really want to help you with today.

You're doing so well talking about this — I know it's not easy.

Just before we go further — do you have any allergies to medicines or foods?

*shakes head*

No, I don't have any allergies that I know of.

Good to know, thank you.

Can you tell me a little about the birth — you mentioned everything went fine, but was it a hospital birth, and were there any complications at all?

*nods slightly*

Yeah, it was in hospital. And no, there weren't really any complications — it went pretty smoothly, actually. That's part of why I feel so guilty, you know? Everything was fine, so I don't understand why I'm feeling like this.

That's really understandable — but please know that what you're feeling has nothing to do with how the birth went. It can happen to anyone, regardless of how smooth things were.

Is this your first baby?

*nods*

Yeah, she's my first. I didn't really know what to expect, but I thought once she was here I'd just... feel happy, you know? Like a real mum. But instead I just feel empty.

That gap between what you expected to feel and what you actually feel — that's such a painful place to be. And it doesn't mean you're not a real mum. It really doesn't.

Have you ever experienced depression or anxiety before — either before the pregnancy or during it?

*thinks for a moment*

No, not really. I was fine before I got pregnant — no depression or anything like that. During the pregnancy I felt okay too, mostly. This all just started after she was born.

Okay, that's really helpful to know — thank you.

Are you taking any medicines at the moment, including anything like vitamins or supplements?

*shakes head*

No, I'm not on anything. Just trying to get through each day, really.

That makes complete sense — and you're doing that, one day at a time.

Are you breastfeeding at the moment?

*nods*

Yeah, I am. It's going okay physically, I guess — no problems there. But even that doesn't feel... I don't know, it doesn't feel like the bonding experience everyone talks about.

That's really important to know, and thank you for sharing that — the doctor will want to keep that in mind.

Who's at home with you — do you have support around you day to day?

*voice softens a bit*

My partner is really supportive, but he works long hours, so he's not around much during the day. I'm mostly on my own with the baby, which is... it's hard sometimes.

That sounds really isolating — long days alone when you're already struggling takes so much out of you.

Do you have family or friends nearby who are able to pop in and help out?

*hesitates slightly*

I have some friends, but I haven't really... I don't want to burden them. My mum lives a couple hours away, so she's not nearby. I just feel like I should be able to handle this myself, you know?

I hear that — but reaching out, like you're doing right now, is actually one of the hardest and bravest things to do. That's not weakness at all.

Do you smoke at all, or have you smoked in the past?

*shakes head*

No, I don't smoke. Never really have.

Good to know, thank you.

How about alcohol — have you had any since the baby was born?

*pauses*

Not really, no. Maybe once or twice at family things, but nothing much. I'm breastfeeding anyway, so I've mostly just... avoided it.

That makes sense, thank you.

I want to ask about family history now — has anyone in your close family, like a parent or sibling, ever experienced depression, anxiety, or any other mental health difficulties?

*thinks for a moment*

My mum had some struggles after I was born, I think — she's mentioned feeling down back then. But we don't really talk about it much. I'm not sure if it was the same as this though.

That's really useful to know — thank you for sharing that.

Has anyone in your close family had any other significant health conditions — things like heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, or cancer?

*shrugs slightly*

Not that I know of, really. My dad has high blood pressure, but that's about it. Nothing major in the family history that I'm aware of.

Okay, good to know — thank you.

We ask all our patients about HIV at this clinic because it helps us give you the best care — there's no wrong answer. Do you know your HIV status?

*nods*

Yeah, I'm negative. I had a test during pregnancy as part of the routine checks.

Great, thank you for letting me know.

Do you use any traditional medicines, herbs, or see a traditional healer? Some can interact with clinic medicines, so it's useful to know.

*shakes head*

No, I don't use anything like that. Just the basics, really.

Okay, noted — thank you.

Before I pass everything over to the doctor, I just have three quick general questions.

How has your sleep been lately — do you feel rested when you wake up?

*sighs*

No, not at all. Even when I do manage to sleep a bit, I wake up feeling completely exhausted, like I haven't slept at all. And most nights I'm just lying there awake anyway.

That sounds really draining — thank you for telling me.

How have you been feeling emotionally — any stress or tough times recently, aside from what you've already shared?

*voice quiet*

Well, everything feels tough right now, honestly. But I think it's all connected to how I'm feeling about being a mum and not being able to bond with my baby. That's the main thing weighing on me.

That makes complete sense — and the doctor will have the full picture of everything you've shared today.

Last one — do you manage to get any exercise or physical activity during the week?

*shakes head weakly*

Not really. I go for walks sometimes with the pram because I feel like I should, but I don't enjoy them. Most days I just stay at home. I don't have the energy for anything more than that.

That's completely understandable given how you've been feeling — and even those walks take effort when you're this exhausted.

You've done really well today sharing all of this — it's not easy, and the doctor is going to have everything they need to help you properly. You'll be seen very soon.

Maternal family history of probable postpartum depression in her own mother strengthens this diagnosis.
2. **Postpartum Anxiety Disorder** — Racing thoughts at night, inability to switch off, pervasive worry and guilt — anxiety frequently co-occurs with PPD and may be a significant component here. Worth screening with GAD-7.
3. **Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood** — Less likely given the severity and pervasiveness of symptoms across multiple PHQ-9 domains, but should be considered if symptoms are acute and situational rather than syndromal.

*Also consider:*
• **Postpartum thyroiditis** — Occurs in up to 10% of postpartum women, can present with depressive symptoms, fatigue, and mood disturbance 4–8 weeks postpartum. Easily excluded with TFTs — important not to miss as it is treatable and distinct from PPD.
• **Iron deficiency anaemia** — Postpartum blood loss combined with poor appetite and fatigue warrants exclusion. FBC recommended.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Postpartum Psychosis** — Currently no evidence of psychosis (no hallucinations, delusions, confusion, or disorganised behaviour reported). However, given severity of PPD, monitor closely — if she develops any perceptual disturbances, bizarre thoughts, or rapid deterioration, this requires emergency psychiatric referral. Early PPD can precede psychosis in a small number of cases.
⚠ **Passive suicidal ideation being minimised** — The statement "she'd be better off without me" was explored and appears to reflect guilt rather than suicidality. However, given the severity of her presentation, direct reassessment of suicidal ideation in the consultation is strongly advised. Patients sometimes find it easier to disclose to a clinician face-to-face.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full vital signs including BP, HR, temperature, and weight (baseline and to exclude systemic illness)
• Thyroid palpation — to support or refute postpartum thyroiditis
• General appearance — affect, eye contact, psychomotor slowing or agitation
• Brief cognitive screen if concentration deficits appear marked
• Assess breastfeeding latch and nipple condition — nipple pain/mastitis can compound mood difficulties
• Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) — administer in consultation to quantify severity and provide a documented baseline score

*First line:*
• TFTs (TSH, free T4) — postpartum thyroiditis is common and treatable; must be excluded before attributing all symptoms to PPD
• FBC — exclude iron deficiency anaemia as contributor to fatigue and low mood
• Ferritin — more sensitive than FBC alone for iron deficiency
